scope: Korean-only level 2.5: thirteen stable IDs, three paired comparison units per lesson; choose by function, context and predicate rather than isolated particle/allomorph drills.
authorship: Original Japanese instructional explanations, Korean example sentences and contextual feedback. Dictionary definitions and examples are not copied as lesson text.

sources.checked: Topic and contrast uses of 는; counterpart 은 depends on the preceding final consonant.
에서 as action location and departure point; Japanese translation changes with function.
한테 includes both recipient and source functions; 한테서 explicitly marks source. Never present 한테 as categorically wrong with 받다.
에게서 marks a source person/animal, with 한테서 listed as synonym.
으로 has direction and tool/means functions; scope intentionally limited to these beginner uses.
로 follows vowel-final nouns and ㄹ-final nouns; 으로 follows other consonant-final nouns.
좋아하다 is a verb, with the liking construction 1이 2를 좋아하다. Japanese を好む is a local pedagogical comparison, not a rule that all Japanese particles match Korean.

좋다 is an adjective; sense 10 includes liking, with the construction 1이 2가 좋다. Both comparison sentences can express preference; drink selection is an original contextual example, not an absolute semantic split.
학교에 가다 and 학교로 가다 both express direction/destination; do not invent an arrival versus non-arrival rule.
한테 has source and recipient functions; chiefly colloquial, 에게 synonym and 께 respectful form.
부터 marks a starting point; time-start contrasts with a time point and endpoint.
까지 marks an endpoint or limit of a range. Japanese rendering depends on predicate: a deadline for arrival versus the end of ongoing work.
밖에 excludes alternatives and combines with negation in the taught declarative constructions. 물만 없다 and 물밖에 없다 have different scopes; original contextual examples.
Particle 만큼 expresses a similar degree or limit; same degree is not a claim of mathematically exact measurement.
Particle 보다 marks the standard of comparison; predicate determines the comparison, not an absolute better-than meaning.
처럼 indicates similarity; the original running example explicitly allows a speed interpretation in context rather than prohibiting degree comparisons.

pedagogy: First show two complete, natural Korean sentences with short Japanese scene labels and explanations. Distinguish what changes and why before practice.
Compare 은/는–이/가, 은/는–을/를, 이/가–을/를, location 에–에서, departure/arrival 에–에서, 에–(으)로 and place–tool, 한테–하고, 한테–한테서, 한테–에게–께, and 은/는–도–만.

Use Japanese meaning/situation choices when both sentences are valid (topic/focus, register, 에/로 destinations, 한테/한테서 sources). Use particle gaps only with an explicit intended meaning or a clear predicate constraint. No allomorph-only drills.

Do not equate Korean particles one-to-one with Japanese translations. 에서 is not simply movement and 에 stillness. 한테 받다 and 한테서 받다 are both natural. 하고 with 전화하다 can identify the other person on the call, not only a physically accompanying person.

Compare 커피를 좋아해요 and 커피가 좋아요 with exact audio: verb 좋아하다 uses 을/를, adjective 좋다 uses 이/가 in this preference pattern. Both express preference and 좋아요 also works for drink selection; not a habitual/momentary split.
은/는 may introduce a topic or contrast but does not itself mean only. 도 adds and 만 restricts in the presented drink/student contexts. 께 honors the recipient while 에게 alone does not.
